summary: On the 144-px fixup rig both sides start from the identical frame (12 rainbow dots on a 12-px lattice, 30 deg of hue per dot), but the port runs ~57-60x too slow AND grows each dot into an ever-lengthening arc instead of keeping it 1 px wide, so it fills the whole strip by t=60 s and its steady state is a saturated, effectively frozen full-brightness rainbow wash (meanBrightness 126.5, 399/400 zero-motion frames at t=120-140 s) while the original stays a sparse 12-dot field orbiting at exactly 12 px/s with a 1.000 s period for the entire 240 s survey.
observations: RIG: fixups.json pins this pair to a 144-px strip (meta.json provenance.fixups.rig.pixels = 144, applies to BOTH sides). On that rig the ORIGINAL renders clean — no compileError, no runtimeError, zeroMotionFrames 1/300 on the 60 s survey. The prior 'orig errors at frame 0' blocker is gone; everything below is judged fresh on the 144-px rig, which is also exactly the original's native canvas size (see the 288-px observation).

ORIGINAL structure: exactly 12 lit pixels at every dumped moment, on a perfectly regular 12-px lattice (indices 0,12,24,...,132 at t=0). Every other pixel is hard [0,0,0]. Lit count held at exactly 12 at t = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 69 s and across a 240 s survey. meanBrightness pinned at 11 (avg=min=max=11) on the 6 s baseline, the 60 s survey, the 240 s survey AND the t=120-140 s late window. brightnessTrend 'steady' everywhere.

ORIGINAL motion: the whole lattice translates toward INCREASING pixel index at exactly 12 px/s and wraps onto itself with a period of exactly 1.000 s. Dense 40 fps dump: t=0 -> head idx 0, t=0.1 -> 1, t=0.2 -> 2, t=0.3 -> 3, t=0.5 -> 6, t=0.75 -> 9, t=1.000 -> byte-identical to t=0. Frames at t=1, 2, 4 and 8 s are byte-identical to t=0 at 10, 20 and 40 fps alike. (Trap noted: because the period is exactly 1.000 s, any dump list on whole seconds shows the original 'frozen' — the 70 s dump at 5/10/15/... s returned identical frames purely from Nyquist aliasing.)

ORIGINAL colour: 12 dots spanning the full wheel with a spatial gradient of +2.5 deg of hue per pixel (= 30 deg per 12-px dot spacing), plus a temporal advance of exactly 360 deg/s. The two are phase-locked so that after 1.000 s position and colour both return byte-identical. Fully saturated (one channel 255, one channel 0 in every dot), no fade tails, no dimming. At 20 fps t=0: idx0 h=17.9 deg; at t=0.5 that dot is at idx 6 with h=213.2 (= +15 deg spatial + 180 deg temporal). motionLit avg 127 — the lit pixels are working hard every frame.

ORIGINAL is time-based, not frame-stepped: at --fps 10, 20 and 40 the 1.000 s period and the position/hue at a given absolute time agree (only the one-frame startup offset differs: head hue 38.4 / 17.9 / 8.9 deg at t=0 for 10/20/40 fps, i.e. exactly 360*(1/fps) apart). Seed-independent (seed 1 vs 1234 give identical stats). Index-only: --rig grid --grid 12x12 produces stats identical to the 144-px strip on both sides.

PORT at t=0 is essentially a MATCH: 12 lit pixels on the same 0,12,24,...,132 lattice, same 30 deg-per-dot rainbow ramp (idx0 [255,0,0] h=0; idx12 [255,128,0] h=30; idx24 [254,255,0] h=60; idx36 h=90; idx48 h=120; idx60 h=150). Same spatial hue law (+2.5 deg/px), same full saturation. A single-frame comparison would score this 10.

PORT TIME SCALE is ~57-60x too slow, and it is a clean constant factor, not frame-rate coupling. Hue rate measured at idx0: 6.33 deg/s (h = 0.0 at t=0 -> 75.3 at t=11.9 s), identical at --fps 10 (6.33), 20 (6.33) and 40 (6.33) — against the original's 360 deg/s. Ratio 56.9x. Positional: the port's leading edge advances ~0.2 px/s (head at idx 0 through t=4 s, idx 1 by t=8 s) against the original's 12 px/s — ratio 60x. The port's full orbit takes ~57-60 s where the original's takes 1.000 s.

PORT DOT SHAPE is wrong: each of the 12 dots is not a point but an ever-lengthening ARC. Its trailing end stays anchored near its start index while its leading end creeps forward at ~0.2 px/s, and — critically — the ENTIRE arc is recoloured every frame with the current hue field, so it is a growing lit REGION, not a stale trail. Proof it is redrawn, not stale: pixel 1's hue goes 186 deg at t=30 s -> 247 deg at t=40 s (+6.1 deg/s, the global temporal rate), and within an arc the hue rises at +2.6 deg/px (the correct spatial law) rather than the ~30 deg/px a stale trail painted 4.8 s apart would show.

PORT LIT-COUNT GROWS MONOTONICALLY to full: 12 at t=0-5 s, 23 at t=8, 35 at t=11.9, 47 at t=15, 59 at t=20, 83 at t=30, 107 at t=40, 131 at t=50, 144 (every pixel) at t=60. Each dot's arc gains 1 px roughly every 4.8 s. The original holds exactly 12 for the entire 240 s survey.

PORT STEADY STATE IS A TOTAL LOSS. Late window (--skip 120 --seconds 20 --fps 20): port meanBrightness avg 126.5 (min 126, max 127), motion avg 0.0 (max 1), motionLit avg 0.4, zeroMotionFrames 399/400 — a fully-lit, fully-saturated rainbow gradient crawling at ~0.2 px/s, i.e. visually frozen. Original over the same window: meanBrightness 11.0 flat, motion avg 13.4 (min 2, max 21), motionLit avg 86.6, zeroMotionFrames 0/400. The 240 s survey confirms the port NEVER resets back to the sparse look (meanBrightness rises 11 -> 127 and stays; brightnessTrend 'rising').

The divergence is already visible in the 6 s baseline: orig brightnessTrend 'steady' (11/11/11), motion avg 13.4, zeroMotionFrames 1/120; port 'rising' (11 -> 20), motion avg 0.1, zeroMotionFrames 119/120. This is a genuine near-freeze, not the sparse-pattern false read — motionLit is also ~1.0 for the port versus 86.4 for the original, and the 40 fps dumps confirm the port's head does not move for the first ~5 s.

The baseline waterfalls make it visual: the original is a field of continuous rainbow diagonals sloping right at 12 px/s; the port is 12 straight VERTICAL rainbow lines that start widening at the bottom of the 6 s window.

RESOLUTION BEHAVIOUR diverges structurally (a real difference, though the 144-px fixup rig happens to be where the two agree on dot count): at --pixels 288 the ORIGINAL still draws exactly 12 dots inside a fixed 144-pixel canvas (lit indices 1,13,...,133; max lit index 133; the upper half of the strip permanently black; meanBrightness halves 11 -> 5), while the PORT scales with the rig and draws 24 dots across the whole 288 px (indices 0,12,...,276). The original is hard-wired to a 144-pixel address space; the port is rig-adaptive.
Neither side exposes any settable controls (probe table: 'no settable controls' on both). Control surfaces match — dials: [].
Neither side binds sensors (wantsSensors false on both, sensors 'off'), so the sensor feed is a no-op throughout.
Seed check: seed 1234 gives stats identical to seed 1 on both sides. Nothing here is stochastic.
feedback: PRIMARY BUG 1 — time scale ~57-60x too slow. The original completes one full lattice wrap AND one full 360 deg hue cycle in exactly 1.000 s: dots translate toward INCREASING pixel index at exactly 12 px/s (one 12-px dot spacing per second) and each dot's hue advances at exactly 360 deg/s, phase-locked so t=1.000 s is byte-identical to t=0. The port measures 6.33 deg/s of hue and ~0.2 px/s of translation. The factor is identical at 10, 20 and 40 fps, so this is a constant unit slip (60 smells like a seconds/minutes or 1/60 conversion), not frame-rate coupling. Multiply the port's time base by 60 and re-check that hue and position stay locked to the SAME 1 s period — if they are not locked the waterfall will show broken rather than continuous rainbow diagonals.

PRIMARY BUG 2 — each dot grows into an arc instead of staying a 1-px point. The original has EXACTLY 12 lit pixels at all times, every other pixel hard [0,0,0], for at least 240 s. The port's lit count climbs 12 -> 23 -> 35 -> 59 -> 83 -> 107 -> 131 -> 144 over the first 60 s: each dot's trailing end stays anchored near its start index while its leading end advances, and the whole span is repainted with the current hue field every frame (pixel 1's hue tracks the global 6.3 deg/s rate, and hue within an arc rises at the correct +2.6 deg/px). So this is NOT a missing frame-clear leaving stale colours — the port is actively drawing a RANGE from the dot's origin to its current position where the original draws only the current position. Draw one pixel per orbiting dot (or clear/redraw so only the head survives).

Fix those two and the port should land: its t=0 frame already reproduces the original's lattice (12 dots at indices 0,12,...,132) and its 30 deg-per-dot / +2.5 deg-per-pixel rainbow ramp exactly, at full saturation, and its motion direction (toward increasing index) is already correct. Structure and palette are done; only rate and extent are wrong.

Steady-state acceptance test after the fix: on a 144-px strip, --skip 120 --seconds 20 --fps 20 must give meanBrightness ~11 flat (min=max), motion avg ~13 with max ~21, motionLit avg ~87, zeroMotionFrames 0, and every dumped frame must have exactly 12 lit pixels. The port currently posts meanBrightness 126.5 and 399/400 zero-motion frames there.

Regression guard for the 1 s period: dump the original and the fixed port at t = 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 s at 20 fps — all five frames must be byte-identical to each other on BOTH sides. (Beware when measuring: because the period is exactly 1.000 s, whole-second dump spacing aliases the original into looking frozen. Use 0.1 s spacing or offset times to see motion.)

Canvas-size mismatch (lower priority, decide deliberately): the original draws exactly 12 dots into a FIXED 144-pixel address space whatever the rig is — on a 288-px strip its upper 154 pixels stay permanently black — while the port scales dot count with pixelCount (24 dots at 288 px). The port's behaviour is arguably nicer, but it is not what the original does; if fidelity is the goal, pin the canvas at 144.

Note for the harness/manifest owners: the 144-px fixup is the right call and matches the original's native canvas exactly (it addresses indices 0..143 and errors below that). Keep the pin; the original is unjudgeable on any rig under 144 px because our engine hard-errors on out-of-range pixel writes where real Pixel Blaze tolerates them.
